warmup.q: A proxy times every call made to the shop's Stockroom. Through the proxy, you call pickBoth("tea", "jam"). Inside the real stockroom, pickBoth calls its own pick method twice. How many calls does the proxy time?
options: None: a proxy only times calls that return a value
warmup.why: The proxy is a separate object, and it only handles calls made on it. The shop's code calls pickBoth on the proxy, so that call is timed. Inside, pick(first) means this.pick(first), and this is the real stockroom, so both inner calls go straight past the proxy. The last section of this lesson shows the two paths, and the Try it in the third section prints the trace [pickBoth].

opening:
A customer at the corner shop buys a teapot as a present. The shopkeeper boxes it, wraps the box in gift paper and ties a ribbon around it. Then Pedal Post's rider weighs it, scans the label and rides off, quite unmoved by the bow. A wrapped parcel is still a parcel, and the courier handles it exactly as before.

In the back office, the manager is too busy to answer the phone, so a receptionist answers for her. Callers dial the same number as always, and the receptionist decides which calls to put through.

Code wraps objects in both ways. The easy trap is to think a wrapper is invisible. It isn't: the order of the layers can change a price, and some calls never pass the receptionist at all.

The last lesson ended on a wrapper that keeps the interface. In this lesson, we'll build two: a decorator, which adds one thing and passes the call on, and a proxy, which stands in front of an object and decides how to call it, with Kotlin's by writing the passing-on. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at the counter, with a teapot in gift paper and a receptionist in the back office. The paper became decorators around a delivery fee, where moving one layer changed the price. The receptionist became a proxy that answers for every method, and misses every call an object makes on itself.

Now look in your own code for a class that implements an interface and passes most calls to a field of the same type. That's a decorator. Does a test pin the order it's stacked in?

Next, we'll stop wrapping one object and start building trees of them. How can a box full of smaller boxes answer "what do you cost?" as if it were one parcel?

sections.h: Decorators: wrap a delivery price and keep its shape
sections.html:
The corner shop charges for every parcel it sends. The rules are simple: 0.50 for each kilometer, 2.00 to start, 3.00 more for a parcel over 5 kg, and never more than 8.00 in all. The rules also change often, so we'd like each one to be a piece we can add, remove or move.

Here's a way to do that. Give each rule its own small object that wraps the rule before it. Each wrapper is still a delivery fee, with the same one method, so whoever asks for the price can't tell how many layers there are. A decorator is exactly that: an object with the same interface as the object it wraps, which does one extra thing and passes the call on. It's the gift wrap. The parcel inside doesn't change, the paper adds one thing, and the courier still handles one parcel.

In Java, DeliveryFee is a functional interface: an interface with one abstract method, which a lambda can implement. Each rule is a default method, a method with a body inside the interface. In Kotlin, each rule is an extension function, a function you call like a method on a type, and fun interface is Kotlin's interface for lambdas. Either way, each call returns a new fee and leaves the one it wraps alone:

Java
@FunctionalInterface
interface DeliveryFee {
    long cents(Delivery d);

    static DeliveryFee perKm(long centsPerKm) { return d -> d.km() * centsPerKm; }
    default DeliveryFee plusFixed(long fixed) { return d -> cents(d) + fixed; }
    default DeliveryFee heavySurcharge(int overGrams, long extra) {
        return d -> cents(d) + (d.grams() > overGrams ? extra : 0);
    }
    default DeliveryFee cappedAt(long max) { return d -> Math.min(cents(d), max); }
}

DeliveryFee standard = DeliveryFee.perKm(50).plusFixed(200).heavySurcharge(5_000, 300).cappedAt(800);
Kotlin
fun interface DeliveryFee {
    fun cents(d: Delivery): Long
}

fun perKm(centsPerKm: Long) = DeliveryFee { d -> d.km * centsPerKm }
fun DeliveryFee.plusFixed(fixed: Long) = DeliveryFee { d -> cents(d) + fixed }
fun DeliveryFee.heavySurcharge(overGrams: Int, extra: Long) =
    DeliveryFee { d -> cents(d) + if (d.grams > overGrams) extra else 0L }
fun DeliveryFee.cappedAt(max: Long) = DeliveryFee { d -> minOf(cents(d), max) }

val standard = perKm(50).plusFixed(200).heavySurcharge(5_000, 300).cappedAt(800)

Read the chain from the inside out. perKm(50) is the parcel. Each method around it adds one layer, a lambda that first asks the fee it wraps, cents(d), and then applies one rule. The tricky part is that bare cents(d). Inside a default method it means this.cents(d), the fee being decorated, and the lambda captures it.

Now predict three prices. A 2 kg parcel going 4 km costs 2.00 plus 4 times 0.50, so 4.00. A 12 kg parcel going 4 km pays the surcharge: 7.00. And a 12 kg parcel going 20 km would cost 15.00, so the cap brings it down to 8.00. The lab's tests check all three.

Then move cappedAt(800) one place to the left, before the surcharge. Both chains compile, and both read sensibly. For the heavy parcel going 20 km, they disagree:

...heavySurcharge(5_000, 300).cappedAt(800)   ->   800 cents
...cappedAt(800).heavySurcharge(5_000, 300)   -> 1,100 cents

In the second chain, the cap brings 12.00 down to 8.00, and then the surcharge lands on top. The gift-wrap picture predicts this: a ribbon tied under the paper is hidden, and the outer layer has the last word. The picture breaks in one place, though. Paper can only add. A decorator can also take away, as the cap does, or decide not to call the object inside at all.

The order of the layers is part of the behavior. Pin it in a test.

The JDK has stacked decorators for decades. new DataOutputStream(new BufferedOutputStream(new GZIPOutputStream(out))) is three wrappers around one stream, a destination for bytes such as a file. Each wrapper is an OutputStream too, and each adds one thing: typed writes, buffering, compression. The FilterInputStream Javadoc says such a stream "wraps some other input stream, which it uses as its basic source of data, possibly transforming the data along the way".

Behavior stacks the same way as arithmetic. The Try it puts a logging decorator and a retrying decorator around a busy courier line, in both orders. Before you run it, guess whether the order matters there too.

try.title: Stack two decorators in both orders
steps: Open DecoratorStack.java (or DecoratorStack.kt). Big Blue Vans' booking line is busy twice, then it books, as booking lines tend to be. Logging writes down each call it sees; Retrying tries up to three times.
Before you run it, write down how many log lines each of the two stacks writes.
Run it with the command below. Then decide: if the log fed a chart of how many bookings the shop makes, which order would you want?

code.title: DecoratorStack.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l05; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Two decorators around a busy courier line. Same pieces, two orders, two different behaviors. */ public class DecoratorStack { interface Booker { String book(int grams); } // the real line: busy twice, then it books the parcel static final class BusyLine implements Booker { private int calls; public String book(int grams) { if (++calls <= 2) throw new IllegalStateException("line busy, try #" + calls); return "BB-" + grams; } } // decorator 1: logs every call that passes through it record Logging(Booker inner, List<String> log) implements Booker { public String book(int grams) { log.add("book " + grams); return inner.book(grams); } } // decorator 2: tries up to `attempts` times record Retrying(Booker inner, int attempts) implements Booker { public String book(int grams) { RuntimeException last = null; for (int i = 1; i <= attempts; i++) { try { return inner.book(grams); } catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; } } throw last; } } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> log = new ArrayList<>(); Booker retryOutside = new Retrying(new Logging(new BusyLine(), log), 3); System.out.println("Retrying(Logging(line)): " + retryOutside.book(1_250) + ", log lines: " + log.size()); log.clear(); Booker logOutside = new Logging(new Retrying(new BusyLine(), 3), log); System.out.println("Logging(Retrying(line)): " + logOutside.book(1_250) + ", log lines: " + log.size()); } }

alt.title: DecoratorStack.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l05 // Two decorators around a busy courier line. Same pieces, two orders, two different behaviors. fun interface Booker { fun book(grams: Int): String } // the real line: busy twice, then it books the parcel class BusyLine : Booker { private var calls = 0 override fun book(grams: Int): String { check(++calls > 2) { "line busy, try #$calls" } return "BB-$grams" } } // decorator 1: logs every call that passes through it class Logging(private val inner: Booker, private val log: MutableList<String>) : Booker { override fun book(grams: Int): String { log += "book $grams" return inner.book(grams) } } // decorator 2: tries up to `attempts` times class Retrying(private val inner: Booker, private val attempts: Int) : Booker { override fun book(grams: Int): String { var last: RuntimeException? = null repeat(attempts) { try { return inner.book(grams) } catch (e: RuntimeException) { last = e } } throw last!! } } fun main() { val log = mutableListOf<String>() val retryOutside = Retrying(Logging(BusyLine(), log), 3) println("Retrying(Logging(line)): ${retryOutside.book(1_250)}, log lines: ${log.size}") log.clear() val logOutside = Logging(Retrying(BusyLine(), 3), log) println("Logging(Retrying(line)): ${logOutside.book(1_250)}, log lines: ${log.size}") }

try.expect: Retrying(Logging(line)): BB-1250, log lines: 3 and Logging(Retrying(line)): BB-1250, log lines: 1. The inner decorator sees every attempt; the outer one sees one booking. For a chart of bookings, put the logging outside: one line per booking. To see how often the line is busy, put it inside, where both busy signals show up.

video.title: A decorator wraps the same interface: the call goes in layer by layer, and the order of the layers changes the fee

sections.h: Kotlin's by writes the forwarding, and never calls you back
sections.html:
A delivery fee has one method, so a lambda can decorate it. Most interfaces have more. A hand-written decorator for Map in Java must pass on every method (get, put, remove, size, entrySet and a dozen more) just to change one. That passing-on is called forwarding, and it's most of the code.

Kotlin's class delegation writes the forwarding for you. Say we want a map that counts how often something is put into it:

Java
// Java has no `by`. The short way is inheritance, and HashMap's insides decide what you count.
class CountingMap<K, V> extends HashMap<K, V> {
    int puts;
    @Override public V put(K key, V value) { puts++; return super.put(key, value); }
}
Kotlin
class CountingMap<K, V>(private val inner: MutableMap<K, V> = HashMap()) : MutableMap<K, V> by inner {
    var puts = 0
    override fun put(key: K, value: V): V? { puts++; return inner.put(key, value) }
}

Read : MutableMap<K, V> by inner as "for every method of MutableMap I don't write myself, call the same method on inner". The object by forwards to is called the delegate. The Kotlin docs call delegation "a good alternative to implementation inheritance", where inheritance means taking a parent class's code with extends.

Now predict. We call put("tea", 1) and then putAll with two more entries. What is puts? The CountingMapDemo in the Try it prints:

CountingMap: puts=1, size=3

One, while the map holds three. The compiler forwarded putAll to inner.putAll, and inner is a plain HashMap that has never heard of our put. The docs say so: overridden members "do not get called from the members of the delegate object". The delegate never calls you back. To count every insertion, override putAll too, and putIfAbsent, compute and merge.

That surprise is also the benefit. With inheritance, the count depends on how the parent class is written today. HashMap.putAll happens not to call put, so the Java version also prints 1. But HashSet.addAll does call add, so a set that counts in both methods counts each item twice, and the Java twin prints added=6 for three items. Effective Java, the well-known book of Java advice, builds its item 18, "Favor composition over inheritance", on that very bug. With by, the delegate never calls back into your code, so a JDK update can't change your numbers.

The delegate never calls your overrides. Override every method that should behave differently.

The JDK has a read-only decorator you meet often: Collections.unmodifiableList. It forwards reads and throws on writes. It's a view, which means it reads through to the list it wraps, so later changes to that list show up in it. For a frozen copy, use List.copyOf. Kotlin's List is weaker still: a read-only type on the same object, with no wrapper at all:

Java
List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(shopping);
shopping.add("jam");           // the view shows it too
view.add("tea");               // UnsupportedOperationException
Kotlin
val view: List<String> = shopping          // the same object, with a read-only type
shopping += "jam"                           // the view shows it too
(view as MutableList).add("tea")            // works: nothing guards it

A decorator works when we know the interface and want one extra behavior. Sometimes we want the same extra behavior, such as timing, on every method of every interface, without writing a class for each one.

try.title: Count what the delegate does behind your back
steps: Read CountingMapDemo.kt. Predict puts after one put and a putAll of two entries, and added after an addAll of three items.
Run it with the command below.
Now run the Java twin, CountingMapDemoJava, which uses extends HashMap and extends HashSet with the same overrides. Predict first: will the Java numbers match?

code.title: CountingMapDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l05 // Decorators built with `by`: the compiler writes every forwarding method for you. class CountingMap<K, V>(private val inner: MutableMap<K, V> = HashMap()) : MutableMap<K, V> by inner { var puts = 0 private set override fun put(key: K, value: V): V? { puts++ return inner.put(key, value) } } class CountingSet<E>(private val inner: MutableSet<E> = HashSet()) : MutableSet<E> by inner { var added = 0 private set override fun add(element: E): Boolean { added++ return inner.add(element) } override fun addAll(elements: Collection<E>): Boolean { added += elements.size return inner.addAll(elements) // inner's addAll calls inner's add, never ours } } fun main() { val m = CountingMap<String, Int>() m["tea"] = 1 // goes through our put m.putAll(mapOf("jam" to 2, "rye" to 3)) // forwarded to inner.putAll, which never calls our put println("CountingMap: puts=${m.puts}, size=${m.size}") val s = CountingSet<String>() s.addAll(listOf("tea", "jam", "rye")) println("CountingSet: added=${s.added}, size=${s.size}") }

alt.title: CountingMapDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l05; import java.util.Collection; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * The Java twin of CountingMapDemo.kt. Java has no `by`, so the short way is inheritance, * and then the result depends on how the parent class happens to be written. */ public class CountingMapDemoJava { static final class CountingMap<K, V> extends HashMap<K, V> { int puts; @Override public V put(K key, V value) { puts++; return super.put(key, value); } } // Effective Java item 18: HashSet.addAll calls add for each element, so this counts twice static final class CountingSet<E> extends HashSet<E> { int added; @Override public boolean add(E e) { added++; return super.add(e); } @Override public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) { added += c.size(); return super.addAll(c); } } public static void main(String[] args) { CountingMap<String, Integer> m = new CountingMap<>(); m.put("tea", 1); m.putAll(Map.of("jam", 2, "rye", 3)); // HashMap.putAll doesn't call put, today System.out.println("CountingMap: puts=" + m.puts + ", size=" + m.size()); CountingSet<String> s = new CountingSet<>(); s.addAll(List.of("tea", "jam", "rye")); System.out.println("CountingSet: added=" + s.added + ", size=" + s.size()); } }

try.expect: Kotlin prints CountingMap: puts=1, size=3 and CountingSet: added=3, size=3: the delegate never calls your overrides, so you count exactly what you wrote. Java prints puts=1, size=3 but added=6, size=3, because HashSet.addAll calls add for each item and the override counts them a second time. With inheritance, your count depends on the parent's insides.

sections.h: Proxies: one stand-in for every method of an interface
sections.html:
Back to the receptionist. Callers dial the manager's number, but the receptionist answers. She may put the call through, take a message, or try again later when the line is busy. A proxy is that receptionist in code: a stand-in with the same interface as the real object, which controls whether and how each call reaches it.

A decorator is written for one interface. A dynamic proxy is written once and works for any interface. java.lang.reflect.Proxy creates a class while the program runs, one that implements the interfaces you name and sends every call to a single invocation handler, one method that receives each call as data. Here is a proxy that retries any method of any interface:

Java
@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
static <T> T retrying(Class<T> iface, T target, int maxAttempts) {
    InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> {
        Throwable last = null;
        for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
            try {
                return method.invoke(target, args);
            } catch (InvocationTargetException e) {
                last = e.getCause();             // unwrap: the target's own exception
            }
        }
        throw last;
    };
    return (T) Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, handler);
}
Kotlin
inline fun <reified T : Any> retrying(target: T, maxAttempts: Int): T =
    Proxy.newProxyInstance(T::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(T::class.java)) { _, method, args ->
        var last: Throwable? = null
        repeat(maxAttempts) {
            try {
                return@newProxyInstance method.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray()))
            } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) {
                last = e.cause                    // unwrap: the target's own exception
            }
        }
        throw last!!
    } as T

The handler gets the proxy, the Method being called (an object that describes one method of the interface), and its arguments. First it asks the real object, the target, with method.invoke(target, args). If that throws, it remembers the exception and tries again, and after the last attempt it throws what it remembered. A retry, a timer or a check of who's calling is written once and covers every method of every interface you wrap.

The tricky line is the catch. method.invoke is an eager gift wrapper: whatever the target throws, it wraps in an InvocationTargetException. Unwrap it with getCause() and rethrow that. If you rethrow the wrapper instead, the proxy is throwing a checked exception, one the Java compiler makes you catch or declare, that the interface's book method never declared. So Java wraps it once more. RetryingProxyDemo, in the Try it, does exactly that when you remove the unwrap:

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.reflect.UndeclaredThrowableException
Caused by: java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException
Caused by: java.lang.IllegalStateException: line busy

That's three layers of paper around one small line busy. Worse, no catch (IllegalStateException e) in the caller will match it.

A handler must unwrap what method.invoke throws. Rethrow getCause().

JDK proxies have one more limit: they implement interfaces only, and can't extend a class. Tools that must proxy a class generate a subclass instead, and a subclass can't override final methods. The Kotlin version is shorter for one reason: reified T, which keeps the type parameter available while an inline function runs, lets the function read T::class.java itself, so callers write retrying(busy, 3) and pass no Class object.

Before you wrap the shop's order line in this proxy, notice that it retries everything. A check of an order's status is safe to repeat. Placing an order isn't: if the first attempt timed out after the warehouse had already taken it, the second attempt orders the bread again. The worked example fixes that.

There's also a quieter gap, and the demo's third line shows it: calls the proxy saw: [pickBoth]. Two more calls happened that the proxy never saw.

try.title: Break the retry proxy two ways
steps: Run RetryingProxyDemo (Java or Kotlin) and read the three lines.
In main, change retrying(CourierLine.class, busy, 3) to 2 attempts (retrying(busy, 2) in Kotlin). Predict what the caller sees, then run.
Keep 2 attempts. In retrying, replace last = e.getCause() with last = e (in Kotlin, last = e.cause becomes last = e). Predict the exception, then run. Undo both changes.

code.title: RetryingProxyDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l05; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Dynamic proxies: a retrying proxy for any interface, and a tracing proxy that shows self-invocation. */ public class RetryingProxyDemo { interface CourierLine { String book(String address, int grams); } interface Stockroom { void pick(String item); void pickBoth(String first, String second); } static <T> T retrying(Class<T> iface, T target, int maxAttempts) { InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> { Throwable last = null; for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) { try { return method.invoke(target, args); } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { // unwrap, or callers see a reflective wrapper last = e.getCause(); } } throw last; }; return iface.cast(Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, handler)); } static <T> T tracing(Class<T> iface, T target, List<String> trace) { InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> { trace.add(method.getName()); try { return method.invoke(target, args); } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); } }; return iface.cast(Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, handler)); } public static void main(String[] args) { int[] calls = {0}; CourierLine busy = (address, grams) -> { if (++calls[0] < 3) throw new IllegalStateException("line busy"); return "BB-" + grams; }; CourierLine line = retrying(CourierLine.class, busy, 3); System.out.println("book -> " + line.book("12 Mill Lane", 1_250) + " after " + calls[0] + " target calls"); System.out.println("proxy class: " + Proxy.isProxyClass(line.getClass())); List<String> trace = new ArrayList<>(); Stockroom real = new Stockroom() { public void pick(String item) { } public void pickBoth(String first, String second) { pick(first); pick(second); } // this.pick(): skips the proxy }; tracing(Stockroom.class, real, trace).pickBoth("tea", "jam"); System.out.println("calls the proxy saw: " + trace); } }

alt.title: RetryingProxyDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l05 import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException import java.lang.reflect.Proxy // Dynamic proxies: a retrying proxy for any interface, and a tracing proxy that shows self-invocation. fun interface CourierLine { fun book(address: String, grams: Int): String } interface Stockroom { fun pick(item: String); fun pickBoth(first: String, second: String) } // reified T replaces the Class<T> parameter the Java version needs inline fun <reified T : Any> retrying(target: T, maxAttempts: Int): T = Proxy.newProxyInstance(T::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(T::class.java)) { _, method, args -> var last: Throwable? = null repeat(maxAttempts) { try { return@newProxyInstance method.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { // unwrap, or callers see a reflective wrapper last = e.cause } } throw last!! } as T inline fun <reified T : Any> tracing(target: T, trace: MutableList<String>): T = Proxy.newProxyInstance(T::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(T::class.java)) { _, method, args -> trace += method.name try { method.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { throw e.cause!! } } as T fun main() { var calls = 0 val busy = CourierLine { _, grams -> check(++calls >= 3) { "line busy" } "BB-$grams" } val line = retrying(busy, 3) println("book -> ${line.book("12 Mill Lane", 1_250)} after $calls target calls") println("proxy class: ${Proxy.isProxyClass(line.javaClass)}") val trace = mutableListOf<String>() val real = object : Stockroom { override fun pick(item: String) {} override fun pickBoth(first: String, second: String) { pick(first); pick(second) } // this.pick(): skips the proxy } tracing<Stockroom>(real, trace).pickBoth("tea", "jam") println("calls the proxy saw: $trace") }

try.expect: The first run prints book -> BB-1250 after 3 target calls, proxy class: true and calls the proxy saw: [pickBoth]. With 2 attempts the program stops with IllegalStateException: line busy, the target's own exception. Without the unwrap it stops with java.lang.reflect.UndeclaredThrowableException, caused by an InvocationTargetException, caused by the IllegalStateException: a checked wrapper escaped a method that doesn't declare it.

sections.h: The calls a proxy never sees
sections.html:
Here is the stockroom from the demo. A tracing proxy, one that writes down the name of every call it handles, stands in front of it:

Java
class RealStockroom implements Stockroom {
    public void pick(String item) { /* walk to the shelf */ }

    public void pickBoth(String first, String second) {
        pick(first);                 // really this.pick(first): the real object, not the proxy
        pick(second);
    }
}
Kotlin
class RealStockroom : Stockroom {
    override fun pick(item: String) { /* walk to the shelf */ }

    override fun pickBoth(first: String, second: String) {
        pick(first)                  // really this.pick(first): the real object, not the proxy
        pick(second)
    }
}

The shop's code calls pickBoth("tea", "jam") on the proxy. The proxy writes down pickBoth and forwards the call to the real stockroom. Inside, pick(first) is a plain call on this, and this is the real stockroom, not the proxy. So the trace reads [pickBoth], and the two walks to the shelf go unrecorded. A call that an object makes on itself is called self-invocation, and it never passes the proxy. The figure shows the two paths.

The receptionist picture holds here. She hears every call that comes in through the switchboard. When the manager walks to the next office herself, nobody at the front desk hears a thing.

The lab's timing proxy has the same gap, and a test pins it. bookTwice on the courier calls its own book twice, the timing sink records one line, CourierBooking.bookTwice 7ms, and the real courier counts two bookings. That isn't a bug in the proxy. A proxy is a separate object, and it can only handle calls that are made on it.

There are two ways to get the inner calls handled. Let the caller make them through the proxy, so pick is called twice from outside. Or move pick to its own object, behind its own proxy, and let pickBoth call that object. Either way, each call you care about crosses a proxy.

The picture breaks on judgment. A receptionist notices when the same caller has rung three times in a minute. A proxy sees only a method's name and its arguments, so it retries placing an order as happily as a status check, unless the method carries a mark that tells it otherwise.

A proxy sees only the calls made on it. Calls through this go straight past.

Decorator and Proxy have the same shape: an object with the same interface, holding the real one. What tells them apart is intent. A decorator adds behavior the caller asked for, such as a surcharge or compression. A proxy controls access to the real object: when, whether and how it gets called, as with retries, timing or a check of who's calling. Collections.unmodifiableList sits on the line, which is a good sign that the names are for talking about designs, not for sorting classes into boxes.

Check yourself. The timing proxy wraps the courier, and the shop's code calls bookTwice three times. How many lines does the timing sink record, and how many bookings does the real courier make? (Three lines, all named bookTwice, and six bookings. Each outside call passes the proxy once; each inner book goes straight to the real courier.)

aside.title: Why does a framework annotation sometimes do nothing?
aside.html: If you write web services, your framework probably hands out proxies like ours. In Spring, a popular Java framework, an annotation such as @Transactional (run this method inside a database transaction, a group of changes that all succeed or all fail together) is carried out by a proxy that stands in front of your class. So a call from one of its methods to another, through this, skips the proxy, exactly like pickBoth calling pick; the Spring docs say self-invocation "will bypass the advice". Their preferred fix is to move the inner method to another class, so the call crosses a proxy. Quarkus, another framework, does intercept such calls, as a feature its docs mark non-standard, so the same code can behave differently in the two. And because Kotlin classes are final (no subclass may extend them) unless marked open, Kotlin Spring projects add the kotlin-spring compiler plugin, which opens Spring-annotated classes so the framework's subclass proxies can override them.

compare.title: A timing decorator for a three-method courier desk

java.title: TimedCourierDesk.java
java.html: interface CourierDesk { String book(String address, int grams); String track(String ref); void cancel(String ref); } // one method changes; the other two are forwarded by hand final class TimedCourierDesk implements CourierDesk { private final CourierDesk inner; private final Map<String, Long> nanos; TimedCourierDesk(CourierDesk inner, Map<String, Long> nanos) { this.inner = inner; this.nanos = nanos; } @Override public String book(String address, int grams) { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return inner.book(address, grams); } finally { nanos.merge("book", System.nanoTime() - start, Long::sum); } } @Override public String track(String ref) { return inner.track(ref); } @Override public void cancel(String ref) { inner.cancel(ref); } }

kotlin.title: TimedCourierDesk.kt
kotlin.html: interface CourierDesk { fun book(address: String, grams: Int): String fun track(ref: String): String fun cancel(ref: String) } // `by inner` generates track and cancel; you write only what changes class TimedCourierDesk( private val inner: CourierDesk, private val nanos: MutableMap<String, Long>, ) : CourierDesk by inner { override fun book(address: String, grams: Int): String { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return inner.book(address, grams) } finally { nanos.merge("book", System.nanoTime() - start) { a, b -> a + b } } } }

compare.note: The behavior is the same: time book, pass track and cancel straight on. What differs is who writes the passing-on. Java makes you type track and cancel, and Kotlin's by inner generates them. That matters again when the interface grows. Add void reschedule(String ref) to CourierDesk and the Java decorator stops compiling until someone decides what it should do with the new method. The Kotlin one forwards it without a word, untimed. Neither is wrong, but know which one you have. And remember that by never calls you back: if the real desk's track calls its own book, that inner booking isn't timed. Kotlin makes the hand-written forwarding class unnecessary; it doesn't make Decorator unnecessary.

worked.title: Make a retry proxy safe for orders

steps.say: A teammate wrapped the shop's order line in the retrying proxy from this lesson, with three attempts. The warehouse sometimes takes 2 seconds to answer, and the shop's code gives up after 1.5 seconds. Before reading on, say what the customer gets on a slow afternoon.
steps.code: interface OrderLine { String place(String item, int grams); String status(String orderNo); } OrderLine line = retrying(OrderLine.class, new WarehouseOrderLine(), 3); line.place("rye bread", 800); // attempt 1 gives up after 1.5 s, but the warehouse finishes it

alt.html: interface OrderLine { fun place(item: String, grams: Int): String fun status(orderNo: String): String } val line = retrying<OrderLine>(WarehouseOrderLine(), 3) line.place("rye bread", 800) // attempt 1 gives up after 1.5 s, but the warehouse finishes it

steps.say: Attempt one gave up on our side, but the warehouse took the order anyway. Attempts two and three are new orders, so the customer gets two or three loaves. A retry is safe only for a call you can repeat without changing the result: the usual word for that is idempotent. Make that visible in the interface by marking the methods that are safe to repeat.
steps.code: @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) // 1. keep the mark while the program runs, so the handler can read it @Target(ElementType.METHOD) @interface SafeToRepeat {} interface OrderLine { String place(String item, int grams); // not marked: one attempt only @SafeToRepeat String status(String orderNo); // a read: safe to repeat }

alt.html: @Target(AnnotationTarget.FUNCTION) @Retention(AnnotationRetention.RUNTIME) // 1. keep the mark while the program runs, so the handler can read it annotation class SafeToRepeat interface OrderLine { fun place(item: String, grams: Int): String // not marked: one attempt only @SafeToRepeat fun status(orderNo: String): String // a read: safe to repeat }

steps.say: The handler reads the mark before its loop, and unmarked methods get exactly one attempt. Why does method.isAnnotationPresent work here, even though the mark sits on the interface and not on WarehouseOrderLine? Because the Method the proxy receives is the interface's method.
steps.code: InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> { int attempts = method.isAnnotationPresent(SafeToRepeat.class) ? maxAttempts : 1; // 2. ask the method Throwable last = null; for (int i = 1; i <= attempts; i++) { try { return method.invoke(target, args); } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { last = e.getCause(); // 3. unwrap } } throw last; };

alt.html: val handler = InvocationHandler { _, method, args -> val attempts = if (method.isAnnotationPresent(SafeToRepeat::class.java)) maxAttempts else 1 // 2. ask the method var last: Throwable? = null repeat(attempts) { try { return@InvocationHandler method.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { last = e.cause // 3. unwrap } } throw last!! }

steps.say: Now make placing an order safe to repeat. The caller picks an order number once and sends it with every attempt. The warehouse keeps its first answer for each number and hands it back for a repeat, instead of taking a second order. The number must come from the caller: one made up inside the retry loop would be new on each attempt and protect nothing.
steps.code: interface OrderLine { @SafeToRepeat String place(String orderNo, String item, int grams); // 4. the warehouse remembers order numbers @SafeToRepeat String status(String orderNo); } line.place("7781", "rye bread", 800); // 5. the same number on every attempt

alt.html: interface OrderLine { @SafeToRepeat fun place(orderNo: String, item: String, grams: Int): String // 4. the warehouse remembers order numbers @SafeToRepeat fun status(orderNo: String): String } line.place("7781", "rye bread", 800) // 5. the same number on every attempt

lab.title: A delivery fee decorator chain and a timing proxy
steps: Run the tests once. All twelve fail with UnsupportedOperationException.
In DeliveryFee, write perKm as a lambda: d -> d.km() * centsPerKm. Then write each default method so it returns a new lambda that calls cents(d) (the fee being decorated) and adds one rule.

In TimingProxy.wrap, build an InvocationHandler and pass it to Proxy.newProxyInstance. Forward methods declared by Object without timing them. For the rest, read the clock, call method.invoke(target, args), read the clock again and report Interface.method.
Catch InvocationTargetException, report the call as failed, and rethrow e.getCause().
Run the tests until all twelve pass. Then read the self-invocation test and explain to yourself why only bookTwice is reported.
hints: Inside a default method, a bare cents(d) means this.cents(d), where this is the fee you are decorating. The lambda you return captures it.
"Over 5 kg" means strictly more: a parcel of exactly 5,000 g pays no surcharge, and a test checks it.

method.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class is true for toString, equals and hashCode on a JDK proxy. Report with iface.getSimpleName() + "." + method.getName(). throw e.getCause(); compiles because InvocationHandler.invoke is declared throws Throwable.

drill.title: A logging proxy from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write static <T> T logging(Class<T> iface, T target, List<String> log) (in Kotlin, inline fun <reified T : Any> logging(target: T, log: MutableList<String>): T). It returns a JDK dynamic proxy that adds each method name to log, forwards the call, and lets the target's own exception reach the caller unwrapped. Then compare. Did you remember the unwrap?

answer.html: @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") static <T> T logging(Class<T> iface, T target, List<String> log) { InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> { log.add(method.getName()); try { return method.invoke(target, args); } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); // the target's own exception, unwrapped } }; return (T) Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, handler); }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: inline fun <reified T : Any> logging(target: T, log: MutableList<String>): T = Proxy.newProxyInstance(T::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(T::class.java)) { _, method, args -> log += method.name try { method.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { throw e.cause!! // the target's own exception, unwrapped } } as T

recap: A decorator has the same interface as the object it wraps, adds one behavior and passes the call on. java.io streams and Collections.unmodifiableList are decorators.
The order of the layers changes results: capping before the heavy-parcel surcharge turns an 8.00 delivery into 11.00, and retrying outside logging logs every attempt.
Kotlin by generates the forwarding methods, but the delegate never calls your overrides: putAll skips your put.
A dynamic proxy (java.lang.reflect.Proxy) sends every call on an interface to one handler. Unwrap InvocationTargetException, or callers get UndeclaredThrowableException.

The limit: a proxy sees only the calls made on it, so an object's calls on this skip it, and it knows only a method's name and arguments. It can't tell a status check from an order that must happen once unless you mark the method.

explain.prompt: A teammate wraps the stockroom in a timing proxy and says: "pickBoth shows up in the timings, but the two pick calls inside it never do. The proxy is broken." Explain what is happening, and give two ways to get the inner calls timed.
explain.answer: The proxy isn't broken. It's a separate object that stands in front of the real stockroom, and it can only handle calls made on it. The shop's code calls pickBoth on the proxy, so that call is timed and forwarded. Inside the real stockroom, pick(first) is this.pick(first), and this is the real object, so the two inner calls never pass the proxy. To time them, either make them through the proxy, so the caller calls pick twice itself, or move pick to its own object behind its own proxy and let pickBoth call that object. Frameworks that put proxies in front of our classes behave the same way, which is why an annotation on a method called through this can silently do nothing.

deeper.html:
JDK proxy classes are final, extend java.lang.reflect.Proxy, and can be detected with Proxy.isProxyClass. Their names aren't specified, but names starting with $Proxy are reserved for them, which is why stack traces show $Proxy0.book, as the demo's did. A proxy also sends equals, hashCode and toString to the handler, so a proxy and its target are different objects to a HashSet unless the handler forwards those methods. The lab's timing proxy forwards them on purpose.

Resilience4j, a widely used Java library for calls that may fail, is a decorator library by design. Its README says it provides "higher-order functions (decorators)" for any functional interface, lambda or method reference, and that you can stack more than one. You wrap a Supplier in a retry, wrap the result in a circuit breaker (a switch that stops calling a service that keeps failing), and so on. The order question from this lesson comes back: a retry outside the breaker retries calls the breaker refused, and a retry inside it counts every attempt as a call. Lesson 11 of this track, Concurrency patterns that tie it all together, builds a breaker by hand.

Design Patterns, the 1994 book that named these patterns, lists several kinds of proxy by job. A virtual proxy creates the expensive real object only on the first call, like the lazy price list in lesson 1 of this track. A remote proxy makes an object in another program look local. A protection proxy checks who is calling. All three have the same structure as a decorator, which is why intent, not shape, is how people tell them apart.
